TASK GIVEN TO THE ENGINEER
On some network file systems (observed on an NFSv4.2 server), removing or renaming a file that
still holds an active lock fails with `EBUSY`. As a result `QLockFile` on Unix can fail to
release its lock file, leaving a stale lock behind.

COMMIT MESSAGE OF THE REAL CHANGE
QLockFile/Unix: try harder to release locked files

On some systems, attempting to remove or rename a file with an active
lock fails with EBUSY (observed on Dell EMC Unity's NFSv4.2 server). We
must drop the locks first, which close() does, then unlink() the file.

The filesystem's behavior prevents most race conditions: for the
unlock/tryLock pairing, if we have not yet unlink()ed the file,
tryLock_sys() will fail due to the O_EXCL flag. If isApparentlyStale()
is false, then the new locker simply fails at locking and may
wait. However, if isApparentlyStale() is true, then we race with
removeStaleLock() in the new locker:

- if the new locker is in removeStaleLocker() and has opened the lock
  file but has not yet locked it, the original locker may unlink() this
  file, but then setNativeLocks() will fail and returns false, causing
  tryLock_sys() to wait then try again

- if the new locker is in removeStaleLocker() and has locked the lock
  file but not removed it, the original locker will fail at unlink(),
  which is ok: the lock ownership has transferred to the new locker,
  which will remove it in releaseLockFile() and recreate after looping

- if the new locker has finished removeStaleLock(), removing the file
  but not yet recreated it, the old locker's unlink() will fail with
  ENOENT

- if the new locker has removed the file and has created the new one but
  not yet locked it, the original locker may unlink() it, which will
  cause the new locker's attempt at setNativeLocks() to fail, print a
  warning, but proceed without a native lock. This is a problem.

- if the new locker has removed the file, created the new one, and
  locked it, unlink() will again fail with EBUSY, which is again ok

The second-to-last case is the only one in which there's a problem:
QLockFile will hold an open file descriptor to a deleted file, which
means it thinks it has locked, but from the point of view of any other
processes/threads, there is no lock.

removeStaleLock() now returns whether the lock file is actually gone;
if it cannot be removed (e.g. another user's stale lock in a sticky
directory), lock() falls back to sleeping between attempts.

On some network file systems (observed on an NFSv4.2 server), removing or renaming a file that

On some systems, attempting to remove or rename a file with an active
lock fails with EBUSY (observed on Dell EMC Unity's NFSv4.2 server). We
must drop the locks first, which close() does, then unlink() the file.

The filesystem's behavior prevents most race conditions: for the
unlock/tryLock pairing, if we have not yet unlink()ed the file,
tryLock_sys() will fail due to the O_EXCL flag. If isApparentlyStale()
is false, then the new locker simply fails at locking and may
wait. However, if isApparentlyStale() is true, then we race with
removeStaleLock() in the new locker:

- if the new locker is in removeStaleLocker() and has opened the lock

  file, but then setNativeLocks() will fail and returns false, causing

  file but not removed it, the original locker will fail at unlink(),
  which is ok: the lock ownership has transferred to the new locker,
  which will remove it in releaseLockFile() and recreate after looping

VERDICT: NOT_OK
PROBLEMS:
- The card omits the main design outcome. `removeStaleLock()`/`releaseLockFile()` must return true only if the lock file is actually gone, including when unlink fails in a sticky-bit directory or on an immutable file. - The card leaves out the errno handling for a failed `setNativeLocks()` during stale-lock removal. EWOULDBLOCK (EACCES/EAGAIN on Android) means a live holder, so do not remove. ENOLCK/EOPNOTSUPP/EINVAL/ENOSYS mean the file system has no lock support, so removal should proceed on the staleness heuristics. Unknown errnos should be treated as held. The card's "must not happen just because setting native locks failed" is too vague to act on.
- The card does not state scope. The `tryLock_sys()` changes (close and return `LockFailedError` on EWOULDBLOCK for a fresh file, and the fstat/stat st_dev/st_ino check) were called unrelated to EBUSY/NFS and suited to a separate commit. An engineer could wrongly include them.

TASK GIVEN TO THE ENGINEER
On some network file systems (observed on an NFSv4.2 server), removing or renaming a file that
still holds an active lock fails with `EBUSY`. As a result `QLockFile` on Unix can fail to
release its lock file, leaving a stale lock behind.

COMMIT MESSAGE OF THE REAL CHANGE
QLockFile/Unix: try harder to release locked files

On some systems, attempting to remove or rename a file with an active
lock fails with EBUSY (observed on Dell EMC Unity's NFSv4.2 server). We
must drop the locks first, which close() does, then unlink() the file.

The filesystem's behavior prevents most race conditions: for the
unlock/tryLock pairing, if we have not yet unlink()ed the file,
tryLock_sys() will fail due to the O_EXCL flag. If isApparentlyStale()
is false, then the new locker simply fails at locking and may
wait. However, if isApparentlyStale() is true, then we race with
removeStaleLock() in the new locker:

- if the new locker is in removeStaleLocker() and has opened the lock
  file but has not yet locked it, the original locker may unlink() this
  file, but then setNativeLocks() will fail and returns false, causing
  tryLock_sys() to wait then try again

- if the new locker is in removeStaleLocker() and has locked the lock
  file but not removed it, the original locker will fail at unlink(),
  which is ok: the lock ownership has transferred to the new locker,
  which will remove it in releaseLockFile() and recreate after looping

- if the new locker has finished removeStaleLock(), removing the file
  but not yet recreated it, the old locker's unlink() will fail with
  ENOENT

- if the new locker has removed the file and has created the new one but
  not yet locked it, the original locker may unlink() it, which will
  cause the new locker's attempt at setNativeLocks() to fail, print a
  warning, but proceed without a native lock. This is a problem.

- if the new locker has removed the file, created the new one, and
  locked it, unlink() will again fail with EBUSY, which is again ok

The second-to-last case is the only one in which there's a problem:
QLockFile will hold an open file descriptor to a deleted file, which
means it thinks it has locked, but from the point of view of any other
processes/threads, there is no lock.

removeStaleLock() now returns whether the lock file is actually gone;
if it cannot be removed (e.g. another user's stale lock in a sticky
directory), lock() falls back to sleeping between attempts.

What if we do get EEXIST? Right now it'll proceed as if the renaming was a success, and unlink `attempt`. Should be `else continue;`, right?

[PS2 Reviewer 02 src/corelib/io/qlockfile_unix.cpp:211]

[PS3 Reviewer 02 /COMMIT_MSG:37]
Depends on errno...

EWOULDBLOCK (EACCES/EAGAIN for the Android fcntl path) means a live process holds the lock. ENOLCK/EOPNOTSUPP/EINVAL/ENOSYS mean the filesystem can't do locks at all so the failure tell us nothing.

You handle the first kind now, but for the second kind "not stale" is wrong: on a no-lock filesystem stale locks become permanently unremovable (silently — same symptom as this bug). Since we already treat "no native locks" as success on platforms compiled without flock, the runtime case should degrade the same way: proceed with removal, trusting the staleness heuristics. In tryLock_sys() the missing handling is the other case: EWOULDBLOCK on a file we just created with O_EXCL means a stale-lock thief grabbed our fresh file so instead of proceeding without protection, close and return LockFailedError to go around the retry loop. For unknown errnos, default to treating it as held: when in doubt, don't delete.

[PS3 Reviewer 02 /COMMIT_MSG:37]
Claude says it can be fixed in tryLock_sys() with two small fixes:

* First, if setNativeLocks() fails with EWOULDBLOCK on the file we just created, a stale-lock remover flocked it before us: close and return LockFailedError instead of  warning and proceeding.

* Second, after locking and writing our data, verify we still own the name: fstat(fd) vs stat(fileName), compare st_dev/st_ino. If they differ or the file is gone, our file was removed or replaced while we were acquiring: close and return LockFailedError, and the retry loop starts over.

Between the two, the suspended locker can't return success on a deleted file: either the remover flocked first (check 1), or it flocked, unlinked and closed before our flock — and then the stat comparison catches it (check 2). Once we hold the flock and have verified, removal requires taking the flock, which fails. On filesystems where locks don't work at all this can't be made airtight, but that's the pre-existing degraded mode.

(unrelated to EBUSY/NFS, so probably for a separate commit)

[PS3 Reviewer 02 /COMMIT_MSG:49]

[PS3 Reviewer 02 /COMMIT_MSG:50]
It could also be the sticky-bit case: in a /tmp-style directory we can create .rmlock but still can't unlink another user's stale lock file. Immutable files too.
